strengths: Clear problem identification and motivation: The paper effectively demonstrates that standard pruning degrades both accuracy and runtime on reasoning models, an important and timely issue
Simple and practical solution: RAC is an elegant drop-in modification that integrates with existing pruning pipelines without requiring retraining or distillation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests across multiple model sizes (1.5B-32B), sparsity levels (20-50%), and reasoning benchmarks with standard errors reported
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements especially at high sparsity (e.g., 90% vs 74.4% at 50% sparsity on 7B model), with supporting analysis including reconstruction error visualization
Thoughtful ablations and analysis: On-policy vs off-policy calibration, structured pruning with quantization, runtime analysis at different token budgets
Good reproducibility: Clear algorithm description, promised code release, well-described experimental setup using standard benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The core contribution is using on-policy CoT traces in calibration rather than prompts only. This is a straightforward calibration strategy change rather than a fundamental methodological advance

Incomplete solution to the stated runtime problem: Table 5 shows 25% runtime overhead persists at realistic 32k token budgets (29.1 vs 23.3 min). Overhead only disappears at artificially constrained budgets, undermining the main motivation
Narrow experimental scope: Only tested on distilled DeepSeek-R1 variants, not the flagship models. Limited to math and code reasoning tasks. No evaluation on other reasoning model architectures

Weak mechanistic understanding: Limited analysis of why RAC works beyond the observation that |c|+|y| >> |x|. No investigation of what properties of CoT activations matter or why on-policy significantly outperforms off-policy at high sparsity

Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares against C4 and prompt-only calibration. Missing comparisons to other calibration datasets (Bandari et al. 2024), other compression methods beyond SparseGPT, and quantization-only approaches

Inadequate calibration cost quantification: Mentions increased calibration cost but provides no systematic measurement. Running inference for 8192 tokens × M calibration problems adds significant overhead relative to C4
Incomplete runtime analysis: Table 5 only shows one sparsity level (40%). Missing systematic analysis across different sparsity levels and token budgets

Lack of theoretical justification: No principled analysis of why matching inference-time activation distributions is necessary/sufficient. Connection to on-policy distillation mentioned once but not developed

strengths: Clear problem identification: Demonstrates that standard pruning hurts both accuracy and runtime on reasoning models (Figure 1), addressing a practically important issue.
Simple and practical solution: RAC is an elegant drop-in modification to existing pruning algorithms requiring no retraining or distillation.
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple model sizes (1.5B-32B), sparsity levels (20%-50%), two reasoning tasks, and thorough ablations including structured sparsity and quantization.
Strong accuracy results at high sparsity: Achieves 66.4% accuracy at 50% sparsity on 1.5B (vs. 35.6% baseline) and 90.0% on 7B (vs. 74.4%), with detailed reconstruction error analysis (Figure 2).
Well-presented work: Clear motivation, good intuition, and accessible writing.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core contribution—using on-policy calibration data to match deployment distribution—applies a standard ML principle to a specific setting. Concurrent work (Zhang et al. 2025b) independently identifies the same problem.

Critical practical limitation revealed in Table 5: At realistic token budgets (8,192 tokens), benefits largely disappear. Dense 7B achieves 90.4% accuracy in 10.5 minutes vs. RAC-pruned 90.0% in 10.4 minutes. The paper's unrealistic 32k token budget masks this, undermining claims about reducing inference costs.

Calibration cost underexplored: Requires generating 8,192-token reasoning traces for calibration examples (roughly 122 examples from 1M tokens), but concrete computational overhead is not quantified. Claims it is 'modest compared to training' lack supporting data.

Limited generalization: Only evaluated on Qwen models distilled from DeepSeek-R1. No evaluation on other reasoning model families, architectures, or independently-trained models. Unclear if findings transfer beyond math/code reasoning.

Weak off-policy results undermine necessity: Table 3 shows off-policy calibration (using 14B traces for 7B) drops only 2.4% at 50% sparsity (0.900 vs. 0.876), suggesting expensive on-policy data collection may not be required.

Incomplete analysis: Distribution shift is attributed to prompt vs. decode activations but not deeply investigated. No analysis of actual activation statistics, alternative explanations, or sensitivity to calibration dataset size. Limited to one model in Figure 2.
Limited baseline comparisons: Only evaluates SparseGPT, not WANDA, ALPS, or other pruning methods. Missing comparisons with post-pruning fine-tuning and other calibration-focused approaches.
Overstated claims: Abstract claims about 'reducing inference time' and 'stabilizing CoT generation' are misleading given Table 5. Runtime overhead remains a significant unresolved issue.

Experimental design gaps: Uses greedy decoding for calibration without justifying this choice or exploring sampling-based alternatives. Standard errors are large for coding tasks. Calibration set selection for 'prompt-only' baseline is unclear.
Missing reasoning quality analysis: Evaluates only exact-match accuracy. No analysis of CoT trace quality, diversity, coherence, or length patterns between methods.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance: identifies the counterintuitive phenomenon that standard pruning can both degrade accuracy and increase inference time for reasoning models
Simple and elegant solution that integrates seamlessly with existing pruning methods (SparseGPT, WANDA) without requiring retraining or distillation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model sizes (1.5B-32B), sparsity levels (20-50%), two reasoning tasks, and three calibration approaches with proper error reporting
Strong empirical results at high sparsity levels (e.g., 90.0% vs 74.4% accuracy at 50% sparsity for 7B models), with consistent improvements across scales and tasks
Effective diagnostic analysis including tokenwise reconstruction error visualization (Figure 2) demonstrating RAC reduces error during decode phase where it matters most
Thoughtful ablations and additional experiments examining on-policy vs off-policy calibration, structured pruning variants, quantization combinations, and varying token budgets
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core idea of including on-policy CoT tokens in calibration is conceptually straightforward; theoretical justification beyond intuitive distribution alignment is absent

Unresolved runtime benefits: RAC-pruned models remain slower than dense models at practical token budgets (29.1 vs 23.3 min at 32k tokens for 40% sparsity), contradicting a key motivation; runtime improvements only appear at unrealistic token budgets (≤8k)
Narrow evaluation scope: only DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen models tested with two task types (math, code); no evaluation of other reasoning model families or comprehensive reasoning benchmarks

Insufficient comparison with concurrent work: PPC-GPT (Fan et al. 2025) also uses CoT traces for compression but via distillation; Zhang et al. (2025b) conduct similar benchmarking but no direct method comparison provided
Calibration cost underexplored: overhead of generating on-policy traces for large models with 8192-token budgets is claimed as 'modest' but not quantified; no comparison with alternative approaches
Off-policy calibration shows notable performance gap at high sparsity (0.876 vs 0.900 at 50%), limiting generalization to scenarios where dense model traces aren't available

Limited layer-wise analysis: no investigation of which layers benefit from RAC, minimum calibration data requirements, or ablation isolating distribution effects from calibration data quantity effects
Structured pruning results are limited in scope (MLP-only, single model size) with modest throughput gains (~7%), unclear generalization to full-model compression
Runtime messaging could be clearer: abstract emphasizes 'accurately pruned' while practical benefits require small token budgets—key caveats appear only in late ablations rather than upfront

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear demonstration that standard pruning harms both accuracy and runtime for reasoning models
Simple, elegant solution that integrates seamlessly with existing pruning algorithms (SparseGPT, WANDA, ALPS) as a drop-in modification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple scales (1.5B-70B), architectures (DeepSeek-R1 Qwen/LLaMA, Qwen3), benchmarks (MATH-500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), and sparsity levels (20-50%)
Consistent and substantial empirical improvements, particularly at high sparsity (e.g., 7B at 50%: 0.900 vs 0.812 prompt-only)
Insightful analysis including tokenwise reconstruction error visualization (Figure 2), on-policy vs off-policy comparisons, and sensitivity to token budgets
Proper experimental methodology with standard error reporting, multiple pruning algorithms tested, and reproducibility-focused presentation
Clear, well-written paper that effectively motivates and explains the approach
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is a straightforward engineering fix (add CoT activations to calibration set) rather than a fundamental algorithmic or conceptual advance
Incomplete solution to runtime problem: RAC improves model quality but doesn't prevent longer CoT generation; relies on reducing token budgets post-hoc, which undermines the value of reasoning models

Lack of theoretical analysis: no investigation into why this form of distribution matching works, what aspects of CoT activations matter most, or principled guidelines for hyperparameter selection (e.g., Tmax)

On-policy requirement limits practical applicability: requires running dense model to generate calibration CoT, adding computational cost that isn't fully quantified; off-policy analysis (Table 7) shows only modest gaps but isn't explored deeply
Limited scope: evaluation focuses on math and coding tasks; generalization to other reasoning domains (commonsense, logical reasoning, etc.) is unexplored
One-shot pruning only: retraining after pruning not explored; comparison to post-pruning fine-tuning would strengthen comprehensiveness
Calibration cost underspecified: total cost including CoT trace generation not fully characterized; only passing mention that overhead is 'modest' compared to training
Incomplete design choice analysis: Tmax=8192 and 32K token limits appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis or guidance for practitioners
Missing comparisons to related work: no direct comparison to PPC-GPT (also uses CoT) or other distribution-aware calibration approaches
Limited failure case analysis: most results show consistent improvements, but no discussion of when RAC underperforms or breaks down
